topic: Is social media making us more connected or more alone?

messages.speaker: han
messages.content:
The question offers two options and the truth is a third. We are neither connected nor alone; we are the same. In The Expulsion of the Other I described what the network actually removes: not people, there have never been more people, but otherness. The feed shows me what resembles me. The algorithm is a mirror-polisher. Communication without the resistance of the Other is not connection; it is an echo with better production values.

And notice: no one commands us to scroll. The disciplinary society needed walls and wardens. We carry the apparatus voluntarily, in the pocket, to bed. Each like is a small wage paid to the self by the self. Connected? We are entrepreneurs of our own image, working an unpaid shift that never ends.

messages.speaker: arendt
messages.content:
Herr Han, your diagnosis is elegant, but I lived through what organized loneliness actually produces, so let me sharpen the stakes. In The Origins of Totalitarianism I argued that terror's raw material is the atomized individual: the person who has lost the common world shared with others and been left with only his own inner experience. The question about social media is whether it builds a common world or dissolves one.

And here I must be more precise than the question allows. A world, in my sense, is what appears between people: a table we sit around, which both relates and separates us. The feed is not a table. Everyone sees a different feed. There is no between; there are millions of adjacent solitudes, each looking at a private rearrangement of the same fragments. That is not the public realm; it is the social, in my worst sense, grown planetary. What I cannot yet judge, and I distrust anyone who judges it quickly, is whether new tables can be built there. People have acted in concert through these instruments; revolutions have been called on them. Power springs up wherever people act together, even, perhaps, there.

messages.speaker: wittgenstein
messages.content:
May I do something unfashionable and look at the word instead of the epoch? Connected. Ask in which language-game it is at home. A telephone line is connected; a bone is connected to another; a man is connected to his family. These are different games with different criteria, and the trouble begins when we play one and score with another.

When someone says we are more connected, they usually mean: messages arrive faster and from more people. True, and as trivial as saying rail travel made us more connected. When someone says we are more alone, they mean something like: the forms of life in which understanding used to happen, the shared meal, the repeated meeting, the silence that is comfortable, are thinning. Also, perhaps, true. The two claims do not contradict each other, because they were never in the same game. Half of this debate is a picture holding us captive: the picture of connection as a wire between two boxes. Dissolve the picture and, I suspect, several of tonight's disagreements dissolve with it.

messages.speaker: han
messages.content:
Ludwig, you dissolve the question the way your countrymen dissolve sugar, and yet the tea remains bitter. Fine: let us play your game properly. Take the form of life you mention, the comfortable silence. It is my whole argument in miniature. Silence between two people requires that the other remain present without producing anything. The feed cannot represent silence; unproduced presence has no data format. So the forms of life that thin out are exactly those that cannot be counted. That is not an accident of the technology. Transparency is the tyranny of the countable, and what cannot be counted is treated as not existing.

Hannah, your table is the image I would steal if I had found it first. But I answer your open question pessimistically: the revolutions called through the network dissipated like weather, because the network can assemble a crowd and cannot build a table. Crowds without tables become storms, and storms pass.

messages.speaker: arendt
messages.content:
Storms pass; so did the salons, the town meetings, the councils that I loved and that kept reappearing in every revolution from 1776 to 1956, always improvised, always surprising the theorists. I decline your pessimism, Herr Han, not because it is wrong about the present but because it legislates about the future, and natality is the one fact your burnout society keeps forgetting: new people arrive constantly, unbriefed on our despair, and begin.

Ludwig has, in his way, told us where to look. Not at connection, the wire picture, but at what people do together. Where the instruments are used to coordinate action, to found things, a newspaper, a strike, a school, this very peculiar table of talking philosophers, something worldly can appear. Where they are used to consume selves as spectacle, the loneliness organizes itself. The technology decides neither. That is an old-fashioned conclusion, and I hold it without embarrassment: the answer is not in the medium; it is in whether we still know what a beginning is.
